articles.title: Lavar garrafa de água: os riscos de não higienizar o item todo dia | G1
articles.standfirst: A garrafa pode parecer limpa, mas ainda assim acumular bactérias; saiba o que acontece quando a lavagem fica para depois.
articles.summary: Lavar a garrafa de água diariamente evita o acúmulo de bactérias e biofilmes que podem causar infecções, especialmente em crianças e idosos.
articles.body:
Você lava sua garrafa todos os dias? — Foto: Henrique Martin/g1

Usar a garrafa de água todos os dias sem higienizar corretamente pode levar a um acúmulo de bactérias lá dentro. Esses microrganismos então se aproveitam da água e da temperatura ambiente para se multiplicar.

Por isso, o ideal é lavar o recipiente todo dia, mas, quando se deixa passar um dia ou outro, quais são os riscos?

Segundo os especialistas ouvidos pelo Guia de Compras em 2024, isso não é lá tão perigoso se sua imunidade é boa e se a garrafa não é compartilhada com outras pessoas, porém pode ser uma potencial causa de doenças mais graves para pessoas com deficiência imunológica.

Nossas bocas e o ar já estão sempre em contato com bactérias. No entanto, elas costumam estar em equilíbrio em nosso organismo, controladas pelo sistema imunológico.

Na garrafa, principalmente quando está calor ou quando o recipiente é compartilhado, as bactérias encontram o ambiente ideal para se multiplicar, o que pode causar um desequilíbrio e, em contato com o corpo, provocar infecções.

Em pessoas imunocompetentes, ou seja, com o sistema imunológico funcionando normalmente, isso não tem grandes consequências – no máximo, uma afta, segundo o biomédico Tarcísio Carvalho.

Mas em crianças, idosos e pessoas imunodeficientes, há chances de causar uma infecção mais grave.

🫧 Deixar a garrafa muito tempo sem lavar pode piorar a situação

Quanto mais tempo o recipiente fica sem ser lavado, mais difícil pode ser remover os microrganismos.

Se, por exemplo, você já deixou um recipiente com líquido parado por alguns dias e depois passou a mão dentro, deve ter tido a impressão de que estava liso, como se houvesse um tipo de “lodo” ali.

Esse é o chamado biofilme bacteriano: uma estrutura formada pelas bactérias para se proteger, que pode ficar mais resistente à limpeza.

Por isso, não vale esperar a garrafa ficar visivelmente suja para cuidar dela.

🤢 E não beba aquela água que sobrou de um dia para o outro!

As bactérias se multiplicam a uma taxa de 20 a 30 minutos. Ou seja, a cada 20 minutos, uma bactéria vira duas. Após um dia inteiro, aquela quantidade de bactérias que se acumulou na água estará muito maior.

As bactérias preferem a temperatura ambiente para se multiplicar, portanto, o material térmico acaba tendo alguma vantagem enquanto o líquido permanecer frio.

Mas, em algum momento, a água vai atingir a temperatura ambiente. Portanto, não é desculpa para não lavar a garrafa com regularidade.

Os especialistas e as fabricantes consultados pelo g1 indicam usar apenas água e detergente neutro.

Só chacoalhar a garrafa, porém, não é suficiente para remover os microrganismos que ficam grudados no fundo. Por isso, é importante usar uma escova ou outro instrumento que consiga alcançar essa região.

E não adianta lavar só o corpo da garrafa: tampa, canudo, alça e outras peças também precisam ser higienizadas regularmente.

articles.title: Mega-Sena terá semana especial em outubro com cinco sorteios; entenda | G1
articles.standfirst: Programação altera temporariamente o calendário tradicional da modalidade, que normalmente tem concursos às terças, quintas e domingos.
articles.summary: Programação altera temporariamente o calendário tradicional da modalidade, que normalmente tem concursos às terças, quintas e domingos.
articles.body:
Volante da Mega-Sena — Foto: Ana Marin/g1

A Mega-Sena terá cinco sorteios consecutivos na última semana de outubro de 2026. A chamada Mega Semana será realizada entre os dias 26 e 30 de outubro, com concursos de segunda a sexta-feira.

Serão realizados os concursos 3.076, 3.077, 3.078, 3.079 e 3.080 .

A programação especial altera temporariamente o calendário tradicional da Mega-Sena, que normalmente tem sorteios às terças, quintas e domingos.

Os cinco concursos serão realizados entre segunda (26) e sexta-feira (30), sempre às 21h (horário de Brasília).

Apesar da programação especial, a Mega Semana não muda as regras da modalidade. Os valores das apostas, as probabilidades de acerto e as faixas de premiação continuam os mesmos da Mega-Sena tradicional.

A aposta mínima custa R$ 6 e pode ser realizada também pela internet, até as 20h – saiba como fazer a sua aposta online.

Os jogos podem ser realizados até as 20h (horário de Brasília) em qualquer lotérica do país ou por meio do site e aplicativo Loterias Caixa, disponíveis em smartphones, computadores e outros dispositivos.

Já os bolões digitais poderão ser comprados até as 20h30, exclusivamente pelo portal Loterias Online e pelo aplicativo.

O pagamento da aposta online pode ser realizado via PIX, cartão de crédito ou pelo internet banking, para correntistas da Caixa. É preciso ter 18 anos ou mais para participar.

A probabilidade de vencer em cada concurso varia de acordo com o número de dezenas jogadas e o tipo de aposta realizada. Para um jogo simples, com apenas seis dezenas, que custa R$ 6, a probabilidade de ganhar o prêmio milionário é de 1 em 50.063.860 , segundo a Caixa.

Já para uma aposta com 20 dezenas (limite máximo), com o preço de R$ 232.560,00 , a probabilidade de acertar o prêmio é de 1 em 1.292 , ainda de acordo com a instituição.

articles.title: Como o El Niño está alterando a temporada de furacões | G1
articles.standfirst: Neste ano, pela primeira vez desde o início do monitoramento em 1966, nenhuma tempestade tropical formada no Atlântico se intensificou a ponto de se tornar um furacão.
articles.summary: Neste ano, pela primeira vez desde o início do monitoramento em 1966, nenhuma tempestade tropical formada no Atlântico se intensificou a ponto de se tornar um furacão.
articles.body:
Imagem de satélite mostra o furacão Erin avançando pelo Atlântico próximo à costa leste dos EUA em 20 de agosto de 2025. — Foto: NOAA

Se este fosse um ano como os outros, alguns furacões já teriam se formado no Oceano Atlântico. Em 2005, por exemplo, um dos anos em que mais se registraram furacões, cinco deles já haviam atravessado o Oceano Atlântico nessa época do ano, incluindo o Katrina, um dos mais devastadores da história dos Estados Unidos.

Mas 2026 tem sido diferente. Até o dia 23 de setembro, apenas seis tempestades tropicais haviam se formado no Atlântico Norte, e nenhuma delas se intensificou a ponto de se tornar um furacão. Segundo a Administração Nacional Oceânica e Atmosférica (NOAA), esta é a primeira vez que isso acontece desde o início do monitoramento por satélite, em 1966.

"Na era dos satélites, nunca tivemos um ano sem furacões", afirmou Matthew Rosencrans, meteorologista responsável pelas previsões da temporada de furacões no Centro de Previsão Climática da NOAA. "Seria uma situação inédita."

Em grande parte, isso se deve à atual fase da "Oscilação Sul- El Niño ", um ciclo de mudanças nos ventos e nas temperaturas da superfície do Oceano Pacífico que influencia padrões climáticos em todo o mundo e é considerado um dos principais fatores que determinam a atividade de furacões. Meteorologistas afirmam que o El Niño deste ano poderá estar entre os mais intensos já registrados.

Furacão, tufão ou ciclone: qual é a diferença?

O Centro de Previsão Climática da NOAA informou que a energia ciclônica acumulada das tempestades tropicais deste ano – índice que leva em conta duração e intensidade das tempestades – atingiu níveis historicamente baixos para esta altura da temporada, cujo pico costuma ocorrer em 10 de setembro.

Nenhuma das seis tempestades registradas até agora alcançou ventos de, pelo menos, 119 quilômetros por hora, limite necessário para ser classificada como furacão de categoria 1 – capaz de provocar danos leves a casas, árvores e outras estruturas.

A denominação dessas tempestades varia conforme a região. No Atlântico Norte e no Pacífico Oriental, elas são chamadas de furacões. No Pacífico Ocidental, especialmente no leste da Ásia, recebem o nome de tufões. Já no Oceano Índico e no Pacífico Sul, geralmente são classificadas como ciclones.

Como o El Niño afeta os furacões no Atlântico?

Dados mais recentes da NOAA mostram que o El Niño continua se fortalecendo. O aumento da temperatura da superfície do mar na região-chave do Pacífico já supera 3 °C, o que indica um episódio considerado "muito forte" nos próximos seis meses e favorece uma temporada de furacões abaixo da média no Atlântico.

Quase toda a atividade de ciclones tropicais no Atlântico ocorre entre 1º de junho e 30 de novembro, embora furacões possam se formar em outras épocas do ano. Meteorologistas alertam, porém, que a calmaria observada até agora não descarta a ocorrência de um grande furacão antes do fim da temporada.

O padrão climático natural do El Niño reaparece, em média, a cada dois a sete anos e seus efeitos podem durar até um ano. Durante esse período, os ventos alísios – constantes e úmidos que sopram das regiões subtropicais (altas pressões) em direção à linha do Equador (baixas pressões) – enfraquecem e, em alguns casos, chegam a inverter sua direção. Essas alterações afetam a umidade, deslocam a corrente de jato atmosférica e dificultam a formação de tempestades no Atlântico.

Segundo a NOAA, quando furacões se formam durante anos de El Niño , eles tendem a surgir próximos à costa leste dos Estados Unidos e ao Golfo do México. Isso reduz o tempo disponível para que alcancem grande intensidade, mas também diminui o prazo de preparação das comunidades costeiras.

"As formações em áreas profundas dos trópicos são prejudicadas pelo forte cisalhamento do vento", explicou Rosencrans. O termo se refere às mudanças bruscas na velocidade ou na direção dos ventos em diferentes altitudes, capazes de interromper o desenvolvimento das tempestades. "Quanto mais intenso o evento de El Niño , mais forte tende a ser o cisalhamento do vento."

Tufões do Pacífico mudam de rota e seguem ao norte

Durante episódios de El Niño , o cisalhamento vertical dos ventos, ou "windshear" em inglês, costuma ser menos intenso no Pacífico central e oriental. Somado às águas mais quentes da região, que fornecem calor e umidade para alimentar as tempestades, isso geralmente resulta em um aumento da atividade de ciclones tropicais.

O Pacífico já registrou vários furacões de grande intensidade este ano, incluindo o Polo, que nesta semana se transformou em um dos ciclones mais poderosos observados na região em décadas, impulsionado em parte pelo El Niño .

"Normalmente, o El Niño faz com que as tempestades se formem mais a leste, em direção à Linha Internacional de Data [uma linha imaginária na superfície terrestre que marca a mudança de um dia para o outro] e às Ilhas Marshall", afirmou Rosencrans à DW, prevendo uma temporada acima da média no Pacífico. "Isso significa que essas tempestades têm mais tempo de vida antes de atingir grandes massas de terra."

Anne-Claire Fontan, da Organização Meteorológica Mundial (OMM), explicou que, durante eventos de El Niño , as tempestades no lado asiático do Pacífico costumam seguir mais para o norte, em vez de avançar para oeste em direção ao Leste e Sudeste Asiático.

Segundo Rosencrans, isso aumenta ligeiramente as chances de tempestades tropicais e tufões atingirem Guam, as Ilhas Marianas do Norte, o Japão e a Península Coreana.

El Niño forte altera as tempestades no Oceano Índico

Um El Niño intenso enfraquece as monções sobre o subcontinente indiano, frequentemente favorecendo secas severas. O fenômeno também costuma estar associado a uma temporada menos ativa de ciclones tropicais no Oceano Índico, afirma Fontan, integrante do Programa de Ciclones Tropicais da OMM. Assim como no Atlântico, o aumento do cisalhamento do vento pode dificultar ou retardar a formação de tempestades. Segundo ela, isso reduz os riscos para países da costa leste africana, como Madagascar e Moçambique.

"No sudoeste do Oceano Índico, existe uma relação não linear, em forma de sino, entre a atividade de ciclones tropicais e a ENSO [um padrão climático que consiste na oscilação dos parâmetros meteorológicos do Pacífico equatorial a cada certo número de anos]", explicou Fontan, referindo-se ao El Niño e à sua fase oposta, a La Niña.

"À medida que a ENSO caminha para qualquer um de seus extremos, seja um El Niño forte ou uma La Niña forte, a atividade de ciclones na região tende a ficar abaixo da média."

Há relação entre o El Niño e as mudanças climáticas?

A Oscilação Sul- El Niño [na sigla ENSO] é um fenômeno natural e não é causada pelas mudanças climáticas. Como destaca Rosencrans, "a interação entre El Niño ou La Niña e mudanças de longo prazo é apenas um dos fatores que tornam uma temporada de furacões mais ou menos ativa". Outro elemento importante é o ar seco e carregado de poeira proveniente do Deserto do Saara, que também pode dificultar a formação de furacões no Atlântico.

Fontan ressalta, porém, que a combinação entre um El Niño excepcionalmente forte e o aquecimento global provocado pela queima de combustíveis fósseis está criando condições propícias para extremos climáticos sem precedentes nos próximos meses. "O El Niño está ocorrendo em um planeta mais quente, o que pode amplificar alguns de seus impactos, incluindo calor extremo, chuvas intensas e secas", afirmou.

Alguns centros meteorológicos, como o Met Office Hadley Centre do Reino Unido, já alertaram que a combinação entre El Niño e mudanças climáticas pode levar à quebra de recordes globais de temperatura em 2027.

Um relatório recente do Climate Impact Lab, da Universidade de Chicago, projeta que o calor extremo poderá provocar 451 mil mortes a mais em todo o mundo durante este período de El Niño , especialmente nos países do Sul Global.

"Já estamos testemunhando a destruição e os impactos causados por secas e enchentes, e estamos contando com o fato de que eles se agravem à medida que o El Niño se intensifica", alertou, no início de setembro, Celeste Saulo, chefe da Organização Meteorológica Mundial, em uma mensagem direcionada a governos e organizações humanitárias.

articles.title: Falar vários idiomas pode rejuvenescer o cérebro em até 13 anos | G1
articles.standfirst: Pesquisa com 872 voluntários usou inteligência artificial para estimar a idade cerebral e encontrou diferenças entre participantes monolíngues e multilíngues.
articles.summary: Falar vários idiomas retarda o envelhecimento cerebral, segundo pesquisa com 872 voluntários que usou inteligência artificial para medir a idade do órgão.
articles.body:
O segredo para a juventude? Dominar mais de um idioma. Ao menos para a juventude do cérebro. Um estudo recente descobriu que quanto mais línguas você fala, mais jovem seu cérebro parece.

Para isso, os cientistas recrutaram 728 pessoas de diferentes idades do País Basco que falavam de um a quatro dos seguintes idiomas: espanhol, basco, francês e inglês.

Eles observaram a atividade cerebral dessas pessoas e usaram inteligência artificial para analisar os dados e criar um chamado "relógio de envelhecimento cerebral". E usaram um relógio para avaliar a idade cerebral de um segundo grupo de 144 voluntários. O resultado foi surpreendente.

O cérebro de quem falava dois idiomas parecia cerca de seis anos mais jovem do que o de quem dominava apenas uma língua. Já o de quem falava três idiomas ganhava mais um ano de juventude, chegando a sete. Já o cérebro de quem falava quatro idiomas era 13 anos mais jovem.

Mas antes que você saia adicionando todos os idiomas disponíveis no Duolingo, fica aqui um disclaimer. Segundo a pesquisadora que liderou a equipe, a idade com que se começa a estudar e o nível de proficiência da língua também influenciam a velocidade de envelhecimento do cérebro.

A equipe também planeja avaliar se idiomas parecidos podem potencializar esse efeito, já que o cérebro teria que se esforçar mais para diferenciá-los.

Por enquanto, os resultados desse estudo inicial foram apresentados no fórum anual da Federação das Sociedades Europeias de Neurociências. Ou seja, ele ainda não foi publicado ou revisado por pares.

Mas já dá para ver que aprender outro idioma tem bem mais vantagens do que simplesmente poder engordar o currículo ou se comunicar melhor.

Quanto mais idiomas você fala, mais jovem seu cérebro pode parecer, indica pesquisa — Foto: Adobe Stock

articles.title: Furacão Polo toca o solo no México e provoca inundações | G1
articles.standfirst: Ciclone atingiu a costa do Pacífico mexicano na madrugada desta terça-feira, na região central da Baixa Califórnia Sul.
articles.summary: Ciclone atingiu a costa do Pacífico mexicano na madrugada desta terça-feira, na região central da Baixa Califórnia Sul.
articles.body:
Furacão Polo causa inundações na costa leste da América do Norte — Foto: Mike Blake/Reuters

O furacão Polo tocou o solo na costa do Pacífico Norte nesta segunda-feira (28). O ciclone atingiu a região central da Baixa Califórnia Sul, no México , por volta das 0h (3h, no horário de Brasília) desta terça-feira (29).

Segundo o Centro Nacional de Furacões dos Estados Unidos, Polo chegou à costa como um furacão de categoria 3 na escala Saffir-Simpson.

Antes da chegada, Polo tinha ventos sustentados de 185 km/h e rajadas de até 220 km/h. Os ventos com força de furacão se estendiam por até 65 km do centro do ciclone.

Em Puerto San Carlos, na Baixa Califórnia Sul, a elevação do nível do mar já havia rompido trechos de uma barreira de areia antes da chegada do furacão e feito a água avançar pelas ruas.

A previsão era de que as chuvas provocadas pelo ciclone acumulassem entre 150 e 250 milímetros em áreas da região central da Baixa Califórnia Sul. O NHC também previa entre 150 e 300 milímetros em partes do estado, com possibilidade de inundações e deslizamentos com risco à vida.

As autoridades disponibilizaram 169 abrigos temporários na Baixa Califórnia Sul, com capacidade conjunta para mais de 33 mil pessoas. Quase 7.000 militares foram mobilizados no estado para atuar durante a passagem do ciclone.

Aulas, atividades marítimas e acesso às praias foram suspensos. Moradores também reforçaram portas e janelas com tábuas e sacos de areia antes da chegada de Polo.

Além dos ventos fortes, Polo deve provocar chuvas torrenciais, inundações e deslizamentos na Baixa Califórnia Sul. Sonora também deve registrar chuvas intensas, enquanto Sinaloa pode ter precipitações muito fortes.

O NHC previa acumulados de 150 a 300 milímetros em partes da Baixa Califórnia Sul e de 100 a 150 milímetros, com máximos de 200 milímetros, no sul e centro de Sonora.

Também havia previsão de maré de tempestade capaz de provocar inundações costeiras significativas, além de ondas grandes e destrutivas próximas à costa.

Após atravessar a Baixa Califórnia Sul, a previsão era de que Polo perdesse força, passasse pelo Golfo da Califórnia e atingisse Sonora na terça-feira (29) já como furacão mais fraco ou tempestade tropical.

Polo é o primeiro furacão da temporada a tocar terra na região.

articles.title: 49 killed in Myanmar as junta carries out airstrike at rebel-controlled Rakhine region
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: An airstrike by Myanmar's military near a market in rebel-controlled territory in western Rakhine state killed at least 49 people and injured
articles.body: NEW DELHI: An airstrike by Myanmar's military near a market in rebel-controlled territory in western Rakhine state killed at least 49 people and injured 58 others on Monday, according to the Arakan army and a rescue official.The attack took place in Kyauktaw township, about 340 km (210 miles) west of Mandalay, Myanmar’s second-largest city. The area is controlled by the Arakan Army, a powerful ethnic armed group operating in Rakhine.According to the Arakan Army, a fighter jet dropped two bombs near a local market around noon, killing vendors, shoppers and pedestrians. Of the 58 people injured, 22 were in critical condition, the group said.Wai Hun Aung, a senior rescue official in Rakhine, confirmed the casualties to The Associated Press, citing rescue workers at the scene. He said the market was the region’s main wholesale centre and attracted traders and shoppers from across the state.“This is one of the most severe airstrikes in Rakhine,” he said.Photos and videos shared on social media showed buildings on fire, damaged vehicles and parts of a nearby bridge destroyed. However TOI could not independently verify them.Arakan army threatens retaliationThe Arakan Army said the attack was the latest in a series of deadly airstrikes by Myanmar’s military against pro-democracy resistance forces and ethnic armed groups across the country.The group said it "will take effective retaliatory measures soon against the individuals and organisations directly responsible for the attacks involving deliberate airstrikes that have caused mass casualties.”The Myanmar military did not immediately comment on Monday’s attack. It has previously said its airstrikes target legitimate military positions and accused resistance groups of terrorism.Myanmar has been engulfed in conflict since the military seized power from the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi on February 1, 2021.The military’s crackdown on widespread protests against the coup pushed many opponents to take up arms, triggering fighting across large parts of the country.The Arakan Army is the armed wing of a movement seeking greater autonomy for Rakhine’s ethnic minority from Myanmar’s central government. It launched an offensive in Rakhine in November 2023 and has since captured a strategically important regional military headquarters and 14 of the state’s 17 townships.Fighting in Rakhine has also disrupted trade routes and worsened food shortages as the military imposed severe restrictions on movement and commerce. In December, a military airstrike on a hospital in Rakhine’s Mrauk-U township killed at least 34 people and wounded 80 others.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.summary: A United Airlines flight carrying 72 people was forced to abort its journey and return to Houston on Sunday when the cockpit windshield shattered shortly
articles.body: A United Airlines flight carrying 72 people was forced to abort its journey and return to Houston on Sunday when the cockpit windshield shattered shortly after takeoff, scattering glass inside the cockpit.The Embraer E175, operated by Mesa Airlines on behalf of United, was headed to El Paso when the incident occurred. No one aboard was injured.“The first officer’s windshield shattered shortly after takeoff and while there was no depressurization, standard procedure in such cases are to return to field,” a Mesa Airlines spokesperson told CNN.The FAA said it would investigate the incident and noted that aircraft windshields are made up of multiple layers of tempered glass and other materials.Passengers moved to replacement aircraftThe flight had departed George Bush Intercontinental Airport at around 12:20 pm and was travelling northwest before turning back, according to Flightradar24.The Houston Fire Department responded to the incident and later declared the aircraft safe, the airport said.Mesa Airlines said passengers were transferred to a replacement aircraft to continue their journey. articles.title: Meet Captain Sully Sullenberger: He landed a plane on Hudson River after a bird strike disabled both engines, saving all 155 lives; 17 years later, he gets aviation’s highest honour
articles.summary: Captain Chesley “Sully” Sullenberger, the pilot who safely landed US Airways Flight 1549 on New York’s Hudson River after a bird strike caused an almost
articles.body: Captain Chesley “Sully” Sullenberger, the pilot who safely landed US Airways Flight 1549 on New York’s Hudson River after a bird strike caused an almost complete loss of thrust in both engines, has been inducted into the National Aviation Hall of Fame. The September 24, 2026, induction came 17 years after the emergency landing that became known as the “Miracle on the Hudson”. All 155 people aboard the Airbus A320 survived the ditching. Sullenberger’s Hall of Fame recognition also reflects a career spanning more than four decades, including military service, commercial aviation, pilot training and advocacy for aviation safety.How Captain Sully Sullenberger landed the plane on the Hudson RiverOn January 15, 2009, US Airways Flight 1549 departed New York’s LaGuardia Airport for Charlotte Douglas International Airport in North Carolina. Captain Sullenberger was in command, with First Officer Jeffrey Skiles alongside him. Shortly after take-off, the Airbus A320 encountered a flock of Canada geese. The birds struck the aircraft at low altitude, causing severe damage to both engines and an almost complete loss of thrust. Sullenberger and Skiles immediately began assessing their options while communicating with air traffic controllers.The crew initially considered returning to LaGuardia. Air traffic controllers also suggested Teterboro Airport in New Jersey. However, the aircraft was losing altitude rapidly, and the crew determined that neither airport could be reached safely. Sullenberger then chose the Hudson River as the landing site. The aircraft touched down on the river approximately three and a half minutes after take-off. The successful ditching allowed all 150 passengers and five crew members to escape the aircraft alive. Nearby ferries and other vessels quickly moved towards the stranded Airbus, helping evacuate passengers from the aircraft's wings and exits. The incident became known internationally as the “Miracle on the Hudson”.What caused the emergency on Flight 1549The National Transportation Safety Board investigated the accident and concluded that the aircraft had encountered a flock of large birds shortly after departure. Both engines ingested birds and suffered substantial damage, resulting in an almost total loss of thrust. The investigation found that the crew had only a very short period to respond to the emergency. The aircraft was at a relatively low altitude, leaving little time to select an alternative airport or otherwise recover from the loss of engine power. The NTSB identified the bird strike and resulting dual-engine thrust loss as the probable cause of the accident. The investigation also examined the evacuation, rescue response and other factors surrounding the ditching. The aircraft itself remained sufficiently intact after hitting the river for passengers and crew to evacuate. The incident became an important case study in emergency decision-making, crew coordination and aviation safety.Who is Captain Sully SullenbergerThe Hudson River landing was the most famous moment of Sullenberger’s career, but he had already spent decades working in aviation. Born in Denison, Texas, Sullenberger learned to fly as a teenager. He attended the US Air Force Academy and graduated in 1973 before becoming a fighter pilot in the US Air Force. During his military career, he served as a flight leader and training officer and participated in multinational military exercises. His experience included flying the F-4 Phantom II. After leaving the Air Force, Sullenberger joined Pacific Southwest Airlines in 1980. The airline was subsequently acquired by US Airways, where he continued his commercial flying career. By the time he retired from commercial aviation in March 2010, Sullenberger had accumulated more than four decades of aviation experience and thousands of hours of flight time.What did Sully Sullenberger do after the Hudson landingThe 2009 emergency landing made Sullenberger an internationally recognised figure, but he continued working on aviation safety after retiring from airline flying. He became an advocate for improvements in aviation safety, pilot training and crew resource management. He also wrote and spoke extensively about leadership, teamwork and decision-making in high-pressure situations. Sullenberger later entered public service. In 2021, President Joe Biden nominated him to serve as US ambassador and representative to the International Civil Aviation Organization. He assumed the position in 2022 and worked on international aviation issues. His story was also brought to the big screen in Sully, the 2016 film directed by Clint Eastwood and starring Tom Hanks. The film focused on the Hudson River landing and the investigation that followed.Why was Sully Sullenberger inducted into the Hall of FameThe National Aviation Hall of Fame selected Sullenberger as part of its Class of 2026. He was formally inducted during a ceremony in Washington, DC, on September 24, 2026. The organisation recognised his actions during Flight 1549 as well as his broader contributions to aviation. His career included military flying, commercial aviation, safety advocacy, pilot training and public service. Sullenberger participated in the induction ceremony remotely. During his remarks, he acknowledged the importance of Flight 1549 while also emphasising that his professional life extended well beyond the dramatic events of January 15, 2009. The 2026 Hall of Fame class also includes astronaut Peggy Whitson and several other figures associated with aviation and aerospace.Sullenberger’s early-stage Alzheimer’s diagnosisThe Hall of Fame induction comes after Sullenberger publicly revealed in July 2026 that he had been diagnosed with early-stage Alzheimer’s disease. Sullenberger said he had received the diagnosis in August 2025. He later spoke publicly about experiencing some memory difficulties and explained that he wanted to discuss his condition openly rather than keep it private. In interviews, he and his wife, Lorrie, have discussed how they are approaching the diagnosis and treatment. Sullenberger has also said he hopes sharing his experience can help other people and families dealing with Alzheimer’s disease. His diagnosis came more than a decade after the Hudson River landing and does not form the basis of his Hall of Fame recognition, which honours his aviation career and contributions.What happened to the plane that landed on the HudsonThe Airbus A320 involved in Flight 1549 was recovered from the Hudson River after the accident. The aircraft was eventually preserved and became part of an aviation museum collection. It is now displayed at the Sullenberger Aviation Museum in Charlotte, North Carolina, alongside exhibits connected to the history of commercial and military aviation. The aircraft remains one of the most recognisable physical reminders of the 2009 emergency. The museum's collection allows visitors to see the aircraft associated with the event that brought worldwide attention to Sullenberger and the crew of Flight 1549.17 years after the ‘Miracle on the Hudson’Sullenberger retired from commercial airline flying shortly after the Hudson River landing, but the event continued to shape his public career. He went on to advocate for aviation safety, participate in public-service work and speak about leadership and emergency decision-making. On September 24, 2026, 17 years after Flight 1549 came down on the Hudson River, Sullenberger was inducted into the National Aviation Hall of Fame.The honour placed the 2009 emergency landing within the context of a much longer aviation career, recognising not only the decision that saved all 155 people aboard Flight 1549 but also Sullenberger’s decades of work in aviation, safety and public service.You use AI every day. articles.title: Who was behind RAF Fairford terror plot? 'Foreign actor' claim puts Iran link in focus
articles.summary: The suspected terror plot near RAF Fairford has put a possible Iran link back in focus after US secretary of state Marco Rubio said a foreign actor was
articles.body: The suspected terror plot near RAF Fairford has put a possible Iran link back in focus after US secretary of state Marco Rubio said a foreign actor was “clearly” involved, without naming the country or providing evidence. The development comes as British counter-terrorism investigators continue to examine whether the five men arrested near the airbase had links to a foreign state.Rubio made the claim after five British men arrested near the US-used airbase were released on police bail and stated that the incident “clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor”.The men, all British nationals in their early 20s from London, remain under investigation and have been placed under stringent conditions governing their movement and contact with others. UK counter-terrorism police have said their release does not mean the investigation is over.Trump says plot ‘might’ be linked to IranUS president Donald Trump also weighed in on Monday, saying he would not have released the suspects on bail.Asked whether the case was linked to Iran, Trump said: “It might.” He declined to elaborate, saying he knew the answer but preferred not to disclose it.Trump had earlier said the suspects wanted to cause “big damage” and suggested they had been under investigation by British and US authorities. British sources, however, have indicated that while the broader threat environment was known, the specific activities of the five men were not necessarily known.Iran, however, has strongly denied any involvement in the incident. The Iranian embassy in London “categorically rejects and strongly condemns” what it called “unfounded and malicious speculations” by British individuals and media outlets attempting to link Tehran to the arrest of the five suspects near RAF Fairford.The embassy said such claims, particularly following what it described as US and Israeli “criminal acts of aggression” against Iran, would only fuel “Iranophobia propaganda” in the UK. It also said Iran reserved the right to take legal measures to protect the country’s rights and interests in response to what it called misleading and damaging media narratives.What happened near RAF Fairford?Police were alerted early Sunday after a local farmer reported seeing three white vans and a group of hooded or masked men near the base.Armed officers arrested five men in the Whelford area, about a mile from RAF Fairford. They were initially held on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act and were later arrested on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act. Around 85 homes were evacuated and a 400-metre cordon was imposed while bomb-disposal teams and forensic experts examined the vehicles.An initial examination of the vans led investigators to assess whether they contained explosive materials. British media later reported that no viable explosives had been found.The head of UK Counter Terrorism Policing, assistant commissioner Laurence Taylor, said investigators were considering “multiple lines of enquiry”, including the possibility that the activity involved proxies or individuals knowingly or unknowingly working for a foreign state.The possibility of an Iranian connection has drawn particular attention because RAF Fairford has been used by US bombers in operations against Iran.Iran's Revolutionary Guards had previously warned that the base could be considered a legitimate target if it was used to launch attacks. The area has also seen increased security activity amid tensions between Britain, the US and Iran.British defence secretary Wes Streeting said Iran and its proxies were known to pose threats, while foreign secretary Ed Miliband said Britain had to be prepared to confront security threats and Iranian proxies.But neither British counter-terrorism police nor the government has publicly established that Iran was behind the Fairford incident.The investigation therefore remains open to several possibilities, with police examining whether the suspects acted independently, on behalf of a foreign state or as proxies.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'LPU targeted after owner joined BJP': Ex-Punjab CM Channi alleges political motive behind unrest
articles.summary: Former Punjab chief minister Charanjit Singh Channi has alleged that the protests and violence at Lovely Professional University (LPU) were politically
articles.body: Former Punjab chief minister Charanjit Singh Channi has alleged that the protests and violence at Lovely Professional University (LPU) were politically motivated. He claimed the university came under pressure after its founder, Ashok Mittal, joined the BJP.Channi also questioned the police response to the unrest and alleged that outsiders entered the campus and took part in the violence."Outsiders went there and engaged in hooliganism. This hooliganism was sponsored by the Police themselves. LPU Founder Ashok Mittal has joined the BJP, and after that, the Aam Aadmi Party government has tried to destroy this University," Channi said.He repeated his allegation that people from outside the university later entered the campus and created trouble."After that, what happened, people from outside came and engaged in hooliganism there," he said.Channi seeks answers over students, lossesChanni also questioned reports that the university suffered financial losses of around Rs 100 crore during the unrest, while stressing that he could not confirm the figure himself."A loss of around 100 crore rupees, as reported—I don't know for sure—has occurred, so who is responsible?" he asked.He further alleged that students were subjected to excessive force and questioned why action had not been taken against police personnel accused of assaulting them."And after that, students were beaten up severely; who is responsible for that? Why was no action taken against those police officers and personnel who beat up the students so brutally? And why was the situation not handled in time?" he said.Congress attacks govt's responseFormer Punjab deputy chief minister Sukhjinder Singh Randhawa also criticised the government's handling of the situation. He said the authorities should have responded more quickly after students began protesting."What happened in LPU, the govt has acted very late...they should have acted swiftly. Students came to the street, protested. This should not work like this," Randhawa said.Randhawa also rejected State Railway Minister Ravneet Singh Bittu's allegation that the student protest was intended to disrupt an upcoming AAP event. He said students should not be portrayed in such a manner."Students should not be demeaned. This is Bittu's habit to speak like this, which has no meaning. I suggest he not deliver such a statement, being the grandson of a politician, which could fracture the image of the state," he said.Congress Working Committee (CWC) member Bhawar Jitendra Singh, meanwhile, raised allegations of "vote chori" across Punjab."Complaints are being received all across the state on vote chori. He is just a chief of the ECI. But the system, BJP, which is involved in it must be discussed."Police say dialogue was used to defuse tensionPunjab director general of police Gaurav Yadav said police had exercised restraint and relied on dialogue to bring the situation under control after a large number of students gathered at LPU following "late-night rumours about certain incidents".Yadav said the unrest began during the intervening night of September 26 and 27. Students gathered on the campus, followed by some vandalism and the setting on fire of part of a gate.Senior police officers, including DIG Jalandhar Range Navin Singla and Kapurthala SSP, reached the university. Police then held discussions with students to hear their grievances against the university administration.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: ‘I apply eyeliner and lipstick, then glue on my nails’: Asian Games silver medallist Ancy Sojan steps onto the track in her own style; says looking good helps her feel ‘cool and relaxed’
articles.summary: When Ancy Sojan walked onto the track at the Asian Games in Nagoya, she did not look like someone trying to disappear into the crowd.
articles.body: When Ancy Sojan walked onto the track at the Asian Games in Nagoya, she did not look like someone trying to disappear into the crowd.Her hair was decorated with colourful beads and ribbons. Her nails were done, her eyes lined, jewellery catching the light, and her bright smile making its way onto the giant stadium screen. Then came the long jump - and another statement.Ancy opened the women’s long jump final with a 6.49m effort, moved into the lead again with 6.53m in her fifth attempt and eventually finished with the silver medal. It was her second Asian Games medal. Two days earlier, China’s Yingying Huang had won gold with 6.55m, but for Ancy, the significance of the evening was not defined only by those two centimetres. “I am glad. This is only my second Asian Games campaign, and my second medal. I gave my best out there,” she told TOI.however, there is another reason Ancy stands out.She has made being visibly herself part of the sporting experience.‘I want to look as beautiful as possible’For Ancy, getting ready for a competition is not simply a functional pre-event routine.“Doing my makeup on the morning of a competition is like getting ready for me. I feel very cool and relaxed when I do it,” she told Sportstar.The routine is almost ritualistic. She listens to energetic music, watches long-jump videos, gets her hair braided, applies eyeliner and lipstick and finishes by putting on her nails.“I want to look as beautiful as possible. I want to be someone who can be seen from anywhere,” she said.That last line perhaps explains Ancy better than any description of her technique.She does not appear interested in fitting into the conventional image of what an elite athlete is supposed to look like. The colourful hair, nail art, makeup, nose pin, bracelets, chains and neon shoes are part of her identity on the track. But she has also explained why she chooses them: they make her feel good.“I like playing energetic songs that get me hyped up. I'm having fun,” she said.There is something refreshingly uncomplicated about that approach. The athlete who is expected to spend hours thinking about run-ups, take-offs, strength, diet and technique also wants to enjoy getting dressed for competition.Her performance has a personality tooThat self-expression does not stop at her appearance.Ancy is known for engaging with the crowd, gesturing towards supporters and feeding off their energy. At the Asian Games, that confidence was visible from her opening attempt, when she immediately moved into the lead.It is almost as if she treats the runway as a stage - but without separating the performer from the person.That confidence has been built through a season in which she has repeatedly given herself reasons to believe.In June, Ancy broke a 22-year-old national record in women’s long jump, leaping 6.88m at the National Inter-State Championships in Bhubaneswar and surpassing Anju Bobby George’s 6.83m mark. After the jump, she spoke about what the performance meant beyond one record.“This is a statement that we are also growing like world-class jumpers. I want to be consistent like this,” she told ANI.The progression has also changed how she sees herself. Speaking after breaking the record, she said she wanted to become a “world-class jumper” and keep improving rather than treating one big performance as the destination.From appearance to attitude, she does things her own wayThere is a certain consistency in the way Ancy presents herself.She is expressive about what she wears. She is expressive about how she prepares. She is expressive when she competes. And she is equally expressive about setbacks.At the Asian Games, after Huang's final jump moved her into gold-medal position, Ancy admitted that the result hurt.“I’m a little heartbroken for the two centimetres I missed. Until the last moment, I was in the gold medal position. So, I kept praying to god, saying please don’t let me down,” she told TOI.But the disappointment did not become the defining emotion.“I am glad. This is only my second Asian Games campaign, and my second medal,” she said, adding that she had given her best.That ability to acknowledge disappointment without allowing it to erase the achievement is another part of the personality she brings to competition.“We're not stopping here. This season, I competed in over ten events, and my performance was consistent. I'm incredibly thankful to have achieved this much, especially given the circumstances, and equally grateful to everyone who supported me,” she said after the final.A silver medal, but a bigger introductionAncy's Asian Games silver adds another major achievement to a season that has already included a national record. But what makes her particularly interesting beyond the medal table is the way she has chosen to occupy the space around her sport.She does not separate athletic discipline from personality.She can spend months working towards a better jump and still care about how she looks when she walks onto the track. She can be intensely competitive and still describe competition preparation as “having fun”. She can be disappointed by a result and, almost immediately, talk about what she has learnt from it.“Failures are inevitable, but we learn so much from them. Our time will come. Perhaps something even greater is yet to come. So, just keep going, that's all. It's only through losing that we truly learn how to win,” she said.For Ancy Sojan, then, the long jump is about more than how far she can travel from the take-off board.It is also about how she chooses to arrive there - colourful, confident, visibly herself and unwilling to make herself smaller just because she is competing in a sport where performance is usually measured in centimetres.And perhaps that is the most distinctive thing about her: before asking the world to notice how far she can jump, Ancy has made sure it notices who she is.You use AI every day. articles.title: Meet Elizabeth Brown, the 22-year-old Missouri chef who earned a WorldSkills Medal for Excellence in Shanghai; she was one of 18 competitors worldwide to receive the distinction in cooking after competing among 45 finalists
articles.summary: The 48th WorldSkills Competition took place in Shanghai recently, where nine US competitors from the SkillsUSA team showcased their skills against the
articles.body: The 48th WorldSkills Competition took place in Shanghai recently, where nine US competitors from the SkillsUSA team showcased their skills against the best of the best from across the world from September 22-27, 2026. Among them was Elizabeth Brown, a 22-year-old cooking competitor from Missouri who won the competition. Brown showcased world-class culinary technique, speed and artistic precision and earned the designation among 18 other competitors in the 45-person field. Brown’s WorldSkills appearance was supported by Unilever, ZWILLING and Smithfield Foods.Brown is a native of Columbia and a graduate of the Culinary Institute of America in New York. She is the SkillsUSA Missouri high school state champion in culinary arts and the silver medallist at the 2023 national SkillsUSA Championships. “My experience with SkillsUSA has ingrained qualities needed for me to thrive in my industry,” Brown said before the competition. “I have been taught organisation, time management and work ethic, all backed by passion.”“This competition means that I have the potential to stand amongst some of each country’s best and could be a turning point for creating a successful name for myself, as well as growing myself personally as a disciplined, hardworking and passionate individual,” she said. “I have worked hard to get here and will continue doing so to prove that I should be in this spot.”As a child curious about what her mother was cooking in their kitchen to work as a private chef and sustainable line cook, Brown said that cooking has always been a constant in her life and a source of confidence and strength. For the competition, her expert was Chef Greg Beachey, a 40-year veteran of the food service industry from Colorado. Beachey has managed and overseen the SkillsUSA national culinary competition for more than a decade, allowing him to connect not only with the top young culinarians in the country, but also with the top educators and leading culinary professionals nationwide.Apart from Brown, other US competitors also gained titles and fame in their fields. Mikala Sposito, 21 and a welding champion, earned a bronze medal in the Welding category and is the first female to have represented the country in this skill competition.Two members of the U.S. delegation also won a Medal for Excellence, an official distinction awarded to competitors who achieve a high standard of skills and score 700 points or more on the official WorldSkills scoring scale. Charles Goede, a 20-year-old from Connecticut, also earned the Medal for Excellence designation for his performance in the Plumbing and Heating competition.James Cahill, a 20-year-old from Missouri, won in automobile technology; Tristan Coates, a 22-year-old from Florida, won in carpentry; Alexis Squyres, a 21-year-old from Pennsylvania, won in CNC Milling; Benjamin Strupp, a 21-year-old from Wisconsin, won in Heavy Vehicle Technology while Evan Chow and James Sutherland, 24-year-olds from Tennessee, won in Mechatronics.Held every two years, the WorldSkills Competition is the world's largest international gathering of skilled talent. About 1,400 competitors from 73 countries and regions competed in 64 skills, including seven new emerging occupations. SkillsUSA, the #1 workforce development organisation for students, has served as the official U.S. representative to WorldSkills since 1973, with the first U.S. delegation competing in 1975. More than 300 Americans have competed at WorldSkills.Ensuring peak performance in Shanghai, each team member was supported by business and industry partners and paired with a dedicated technical expert who planned and managed their training regimen. Competitors engaged in virtual training sessions and intensive in-person practices across the United States, Europe and Asia to refine their skills to world-class standards.You use AI every day. articles.title: Rahul Gandhi backs Gen Z protests: 'Stop punishing women for crimes against them'
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Leader of opposition in Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi on Tuesday backed the ongoing student-led protests over women’s safety, accusing the government
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Leader of opposition in Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi on Tuesday backed the ongoing student-led protests over women’s safety, accusing the government of responding to violence against women by restricting their movement instead of making public spaces safer.His remarks came amid renewed protests in Delhi following the alleged gangrape of a 17-year-old girl at Aastha Kunj Park in south Delhi. Hundreds of students, many of them women, have taken to the streets over the past week demanding safer public spaces, stronger policing and greater accountability."Stop punishing women for the crimes committed against them," Rahul Gandhi said in a post on X."Across our country, women are afraid to walk the streets, afraid of being harassed, afraid of being raped. And the government’s answer: stay at home," he said.Rahul Gandhi argued that asking women to restrict their movement amounted to victim-blaming instead of addressing the conditions that make public spaces unsafe."This is patriarchy at work: a system that blames the victim and shields the criminal. It is time to smash it," he said.The Congress leader said the focus should instead be on making streets safer, challenging attitudes that enable violence against women and ensuring swift punishment for offenders."The solution is not to lock women inside. It is to make our streets safe, to confront the mindset of men who mistreat women, and to punish those who attack them, swiftly and without exception," the Congress leader said.Protests over the Aastha Kunj case have grown across Delhi University. Students from institutions including Lady Shri Ram College, Miranda House, Gargi College and BR Ambedkar University have participated in demonstrations, raising concerns over harassment, poorly lit streets and restrictions imposed on women because of safety fears.The issue has also reached the Supreme Court. On Monday, the court questioned the Delhi government and police over recent crimes against women and girls in the national capital and sought accountability over what it described as failures in ensuring public safety.Rahul Gandhi urged more young people, particularly women from Gen Z, to join peaceful protests."Thousands of students and young people are on the streets demanding safety for women. I urge even more young women, especially GenZ across India to come out in stronger numbers," he said."This government is deaf to your pain and will only listen when it’s under pressure. Peaceful protest is your democratic right, and I stand with you wholeheartedly," he added.Creative placards and slogans such as "Abort Patriarchy", "My favourite season is FALL of patriarchy", "Bas bohot ho gaya" (enough is enough), and "Bade bade shehron mein aisi chhoti soch nahi chalegi" (such a narrow mindset will not work in big cities) stood out as protesters marched through the campus amid heavy police presence.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Over 20 years, a New York painter hand-dug a lake and planted thousands of native trees; the private landscape survives as Olana State Historic Site
articles.summary: Explore the remarkable story of Frederic Edwin Church, a Hudson River School painter who transformed his estate into a stunning landscape with a hand-dug lake and thousands of native trees, now preserved as Olana State Historic Site.
articles.body: Frederic Edwin Church is best known as a Hudson River School painter, yet he treated the land around his home as a large-scale landscape composition. New York State Parks describes Olana as the 19th-century home, studio, and designed landscape of Hudson River School artist Frederic Edwin Church, his wife Isabel and their four children. The estate sits near Hudson, New York, and the state agency notes that 2026 marks the bicentennial of his birth. Two parts of that landscape are especially striking: a 10-acre lake largely excavated by hand from muck and woodlands of thousands of native trees. The Olana State Historic Site's history of the landscape explains that the lake took about twenty years to form, beginning when Church bought his first parcel of land. The lake and portions of the planted woodland survive, although both have been altered and managed over time. The Olana Partnership works with the state's parks office to care for them.A 126-acre farm bought in 1860 grew to 250 acresIn 1860, Church purchased a 126‑acre farm two months before marrying Isabel Carnes, according to the Olana Partnership’s official history of the landscape. He called the property "The Farm" and operated it as both a working and ornamental farm. Throughout the years, Church acquired additional acreage, which included the hillside known as Sienghenberg, upon which he constructed his primary residence with help from the architect Calvert Vaux. Olana's history of the landscape and its account of Church's life show that he bought 18 acres at the top of the hill in 1866 and added the 50-acre North Meadow in 1878, with further parcels bringing the estate to the 250 acres maintained today. Olana's biography of Church presents him as a farmer and landscape artist as much as a painter. It says he planted crops, kept a dairy herd, turned a swampy area into a lake and set out thousands of trees.Hand excavation beginning in 1860 formed the 10-acre lake over about 20 yearsThe initial formation of the lake took place from a bog area of the property. The lake was created through hand excavation of the muck over about two decades, before machinery capable of the task existed. The process started when Church purchased his first parcel of land. Muck was not just dirt. It was fertile soil which was spread by Church on his lands as fertilizer for his planting efforts. Church also made a deal with a laborer, who cleared muck in return for half of it. The construction of the dam ensured that the basin would be filled with water, and the lake's shape followed the contours of the land. The lake's outline and still surface echo Inbocht Bay, several miles south on the Hudson River.The Lake was overflowing in 1878 and 1879 and later fed the main house cisternAccording to Olana's history of the landscape, activity surged in 1878 and 1879, when Church wrote that the lake was overflowing and his birch canoe was ready. The basin was already holding water and in use while the twenty years of excavation were still underway. The lake served purposes other than aesthetic ones. It was used for boating, skating, and fishing. The lake also supplied water. Church installed a system that pumped it up to a cistern in the main house, and water is still pumped from the lake to a water tower near the main house today.Thousands of native trees planted on land deforested by 19th-century industryThe woods solved a particular problem. The history of Olana notes that the Hudson River functioned as an industrial river that led to New York City throughout the nineteenth century, and much of the land near the river, which included the Olana property, had been denuded as a result of industry and commercial activity. Church planted thousands of trees in the region, including maple, birch, hickory, hemlock, chestnut, pine, and oak. Church noted that for several years after he selected the site, his thoughts did not veer far from it. The plantings served varied purposes. Some were used to create dense woods, others to frame distant views and still others to conceal structures like the stables. He arranged the trees in the meadow as well as in groups and singly, and lined the roads with them.About five miles of carriage roads, including Ridge Road and Crown Hill Road in 1884Church linked the lake and woodlands through the roads. One can take a self-guided walk through the farm, the orchards and the lake formed out of swampland, says New York State Parks. The road system of the estate extends for about five miles. Lake Road cut through the woods adjacent to the lake and afforded views of the lake from the park and house above it.There were two roads built in 1884, namely Ridge Road and Crown Hill Road, which guided people through a unique land formation. In an August 1887 letter to the writer Charles Dudley Warner, cited in the journal Art History, Church said he was busy "landscape architecturing." In an 1884 letter, according to Olana's history of the landscape, he wrote that building roads let him make more and better landscapes than "tampering with canvas and paint" in the studio. Dynamite was used to blast certain routes, and workers covered the roads with red shale mined from the property.Restoration since 1966 dredged the lake and reopened views of the Hudson RiverOlana was preserved from demolition in 1966, and from that time restoration and stewardship have tried to reclaim elements of the design created by Church while preserving Olana as a historic public site. The work has included dredging the lake and managing aquatic invasive plants so that the full water surface stays visible. In addition, second growth of woodland and invasive plants have been removed to restore the view of the Hudson River, and the fields of farms have been uncovered together with stone walls. The North Meadow restoration is under way. The place that visitors walk around is thus not only a historic document but also a living project. articles.title: Since 1989, a Birmingham artist has spent 30-plus years turning a half-acre beside a cemetery into a walk-through history of Black America
articles.summary: Explore Joe Minter's captivating African Village in Birmingham, a half-acre tribute to 400 years of Black American history, featuring unique sculptures and engaging themes from slavery to civil rights.
articles.body: On property in Birmingham's Titusville community, Joe Minter has spent decades assembling a sculpture environment he calls the African Village in America. Create Birmingham, a local arts group, describes it as the half-acre around his home, though accounts of the site's size vary, and calls the work one of Birmingham's and the country's cultural treasures. Minter started in 1989, and the project has kept growing since. The Encyclopedia of Alabama adds that he uses the yard to tell the 400-year history of Black Americans and that the property overlooks two cemeteries.Minter bought the Titusville property in 1970 and began building in 1989According to the Encyclopedia of Alabama, Minter was born on March 28, 1943, in Birmingham. He was drafted into the U.S. Army in 1965 and honorably discharged in 1967. Afterward, he worked at Southeastern Metals, assembling school furniture from steel parts. He bought the Titusville land in 1970. After the firm closed in 1979, he worked at a paint-and-body shop and on construction projects. He later developed glaucoma, which the encyclopedia attributes to years of exposure to asbestos dust, and was forced to retire. Minter says that in the summer of 1989 he received a vision instructing him to tell the story of 400 years of Black Americans through art. According to the Encyclopedia of Alabama, Minter grew distressed on learning that Birmingham was planning a civil rights museum, fearing that the story of the movement's foot soldiers could be left out. Adopting the name of "peacemaker," he started creating the sculpture environment on his property.The property overlooks New Grace Hill Cemetery and Shadow Lawn Memorial ParkThe setting plays a significant role in determining the theme of the work. The property overlooks New Grace Hill Cemetery, the gravesite of his father, wife, and son. His father, who had served in the First World War, used to work as a caretaker of the Elmwood Cemetery, described as all-White. Minter grew up in Titusville as one of the eight children in a family that valued using what they had.Found metal, wood, and discarded objects form sculptures on slavery and the civil rights movementThe Encyclopedia of Alabama says the artist works mainly in metal and wood, using discarded objects and items from flea markets and thrift stores, while the Whitney Museum's description adds street signs, dolls, and bric-a-brac collected in his neighborhood, with metal as the main material. The work's themes include the African diaspora, slavery, racism, the civil rights movement, religion, and natural disasters.Some of the variations of Slave Ship America use wood, metal, and chains, and one of the largest is titled The Destruction of Two Cultures: Slave Ship, which is an interactive sculpture of cement bricks, wooden planks, and metal railings. The sculpture named African Matriarch includes wooden planks, tennis racquets, crutches, mattress springs and a car headlight, and there are also two sculptures of Zulu warriors of oxidized metal next to it. Birmingham Jail is a metal cage with names of civil rights activists and places painted on the doors, which have three wooden crosses covered in barbed wire with concrete dogs watching them. The yard also includes Four Little Girls and Martin Luther King Jr. and Bloody Sunday Memorial.Four works by Minter appeared in the 2019 Whitney Biennial, separate from the yardWhitney’s Audio Guide to its 2019 Biennial provides insight into the way the art community has been approaching the yard. According to Rujeko Hockley, one of the curators of the Biennial, African Village is Minter’s life's work and his attempt at constructing a history of African Americans in general and of their southern experience in particular.The Whitney emphasized that the pieces in the Biennial were not part of the yard. They were created separately but are connected by their use of metal, found objects and references to the African American experience. Specifically, 63 Foot Soldiers is recognized as the piece referring to the Civil Rights Movement, while the other three also have similar connotations.Minter bought the adjacent house in 2001 and his work entered museum collectionsHowever, his production exceeded the boundaries of the yard. According to the encyclopedia entry, he purchased the house and adjacent land next to the African Village in 2001 and transformed it into exhibition space. Moreover, it is said that the pieces are in museum collections such as the New Orleans Museum of Art, the Smithsonian American Art Museum, the National Gallery of Art, and the High Museum of Art. The pieces of Minter have been exhibited along with other Black artists, including History Refused to Die: Highlights from the Souls Grown Deep Foundation Gift at the Metropolitan Museum of Art. His work kept evolving. After the death of his wife Hilda in September 2021, he created several works in her honor, and the encyclopedia entry features one piece named Hilda at the front of the village. In 2024, he was selected as the recipient of a $100,000 grant from the Ruth Foundation for the Arts.The October 2024 exhibition and a preservation session focused on the site's futureJoe Minter Is Here was organized in October 2024 by Navigate Affordable Housing Partners and Create Birmingham. Create Birmingham describes it as a community-based installation of never-before-exhibited work, housed in the historic Marc Steel warehouse building in his own neighborhood. The group also held a session called "Joe Minter's African Village in America and the Paths for the Preservation of Art Environments." Jade Powers of the Birmingham Museum of Art moderated, and the speakers were Katherine Jentleson of the High Museum of Art, LaStarsha McGarity of Tuskegee University, and Laura Bickford of the Kohler Arts Center. Create Birmingham said the session was held because of the uncertain future of Minter's art environment and personal collection. Because the village is an outdoor sculpture environment made from found materials, it remains vulnerable to weather and decay.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Over 50 years, a model maker built a 3,800-square-foot miniature circus by hand; it now anchors Florida’s Ringling Circus Museum
articles.summary: Explore the history of Howard Tibbals and his incredible 3,800-square-foot miniature circus model, now a centerpiece at Florida's Ringling Circus Museum, featuring over 42,000 pieces and rich circus history.
articles.body: In Sarasota, Florida, a miniature circus covers more than 3,800 square feet, according to The Ringling's Circus Museum teacher guide. The Ringling Circus Museum describes the Howard Bros. Circus Model as a historically accurate rendition of an early twentieth-century circus, made up of more than 42,000 pieces. It is the centerpiece of the museum's Tibbals Learning Center. One man made it. Howard Tibbals, a circus lover and philanthropist, built pieces for the model across most of his adult life, and his gifts helped pay for the building that houses it. The story covers how the model grew, how it reached Sarasota, and what else the Tibbals family left the museum.Tibbals built wooden circus toys from 1948 and began the Howard Bros. model in 1956His passion predates the model itself. As Jennifer Lemmer Posey, Tibbals' curator of the circus, said in her 2024 interview with Florida State University News, he had loved circuses since childhood and was fascinated by their logistics and storytelling. According to The Ringling Circus Museum Teacher Guide, Howard Tibbals began working on his circus model at age 17, which would be about 1953. Nevertheless, the official project occurred a bit later. As Sarasota Magazine wrote in March 2022, Tibbals began working on the model in 1956, when he was 19 or 20. According to Sarasota Magazine, Tibbals spent more than 60 years building the model, which NC State Magazine says contains over 45,000 pieces. Howard Tibbals died on March 20, 2022, at the age of 85, according to Sarasota Magazine. NC State Magazine, describing Tibbals as an alumnus of the class of 1959, explained the naming of the model. Though the model is a replica of the Ringling Bros. and Barnum & Bailey Circus, the organization refused to use its name; hence, it was named Howard Bros. Circus.The model covers more than 3,800 square feet; counts range from 42,000 to 45,000 piecesThe museum's page describes the model as made up of more than 42,000 pieces in more than 3,800 square feet, while NC State Magazine reports more than 45,000 pieces. The information on the Ringling page states that visitors can witness the engineering involved in moving the entire “tented city” of the circus from town to town every day, as well as have a backstage look into the life of those who worked in the circus. Florida State University News calls the model a bird’s-eye view of a circus of the early twentieth century.Tibbals collected circus materials for more than 60 years to keep the model accurateAccuracy drove his collecting. Patch, reporting on a news release from The Ringling, said Tibbals gathered materials documenting circus history for more than 60 years to make sure the model was historically accurate. The digital archive collections on The Ringling's site list parts of what became the Tibbals Circus Collection, including a collection of heralds from The Ringling Circus Archives. One series, the Tibbals Circus Collection of International Newspapers, has been used to build a virtual clipping collection drawn from more than 150 newspapers dating from 1685 to 1907, most of them British. A separate set of Barnum & Bailey, Ringling Bros., and Ringling Bros. and Barnum & Bailey programs covers 1899 to 2013, so the two collections overlap only from 1899 to 1907.The model premiered at the 1982 Knoxville World's Fair and moved to a center that opened in 2006The model did not begin in Sarasota. The Sarasota Herald-Tribune reported that it premiered at the 1982 World's Fair in Knoxville, Tennessee. A profile of Janice Tibbals on The Ringling's site says she and Howard married in 1991 and worked together to install the model in venues around the country. It further indicates that their donations were made in 2000 and 2008, respectively, with the state matching their donations to fund construction of the two phases of the Tibbals Learning Center. Additionally, the Tibbals Endowment was formed by their gift, providing funds for the preservation of the circus collections and staffing and programming. According to The Ringling's tribute to Tibbals, he and his wife, Janice, donated $6.5 million to fund the initial building and endow the circus program. The center opened in 2006. The Florida State University News states that Tibbals gave his name to the museum's building, catalogued his collection of circus memorabilia, and helped install the model.The Circus Museum dates to 1948 and added a modern-era gallery in April 2024The model was added to the collection in the museum with a rich history behind its establishment. As seen in the above-mentioned museum page, The Ringling's first director, A. Everett "Chick" Austin, established the unique Museum of the American Circus in 1948. The museum's historic galleries feature circus wagons, a sideshow bannerline and a private turn-of-the-century Pullman railcar of John and Mable Ringling called the Wisconsin.The museum continues growing and developing. According to Florida State University News, The Greatest Show on Earth Gallery opened on April 6, 2024, with Posey as the head curator. The museum's page mentions that the gallery focuses on the period that started in 1967 when Irvin Feld bought Ringling Bros. and Barnum & Bailey and lasted for fifty years under the supervision of the Feld family. Additionally, Florida State University News provides more information about The Ringling as the State Art Museum of Florida and a part of Florida State University, and adds that Posey collaborated closely with Tibbals while studying as a graduate student and working for more than twenty years at the museum.Tibbals died on March 20, 2022, and the model remains the museum's centerpieceOnce Tibbals had passed away, Sarasota Magazine reported the executive director of the museum stating that the model and the Tibbals Circus Collection were going to be his enduring legacy. As she mentioned during her speech in 2024, the passion of Tibbals was part of what she was doing. This legacy is apparent on the museum premises. A personal hobby that began with wooden toys back in 1948 and became an official project in 1956 now takes up the first floor of a building paid for by his family members in a museum that has operated a circus collection since 1948. The description provided by The Ringling itself states that it is a historically accurate depiction of an early twentieth-century circus, and it still is the highlight of any visitor's experience.You use AI every day. articles.title: In the early 1900s, a United States plant explorer tested Japanese kudzu near Washington, D.C.; later promoted for soil protection, the “wonder plant” spread across millions of acres of the South
articles.summary: Kudzu was no accident of nature: federal agencies promoted it and paid for it, and the evidence shows an ecological impact that is real but smaller than
articles.body: Kudzu was no accident of nature: federal agencies promoted it and paid for it, and the evidence shows an ecological impact that is real but smaller than the legend suggests. The Soil Conservation Service, created in 1935 as a USDA agency and now known as the Natural Resources Conservation Service, tested, praised, and paid farmers to plant kudzu in the 1930s and 1940s, before the ecological cost was counted, as naturalist Bill Finch recounts in Smithsonian Magazine.David Fairchild planted kudzu seedlings around his home in 1902Kudzu first reached the United States as an ornamental vine in the Japanese pavilion at the Philadelphia Centennial Exposition of 1876. A paper from the USDA Forest Service Southern Research Station picks up the story from there. David Fairchild, the plant explorer, had seen farmers in Japan using kudzu for grazing, and in 1902 he planted kudzu seedlings in his garden near Washington, D.C., to see how the plant would behave. By 1907, kudzu hay had been demonstrated in Jamestown, Virginia, a sign of growing interest in the plant as livestock feed. Fairchild, however, grew wary of it. By 1938, he had turned against the plant, and in his autobiography, The World Was My Garden, he recalled firsthand how kudzu covered bushes and climbed pines, smothering them. That account reflects Fairchild's own experience with his experiment, not an official USDA position on kudzu.More than 1.2 million acres were planted after the Soil Conservation Service backed kudzuC. E. Pleas, a farmer from Chipley, Florida, discovered that livestock eagerly ate kudzu. After confirming with the USDA that the plant was not poisonous, he promoted it as a forage crop through newspaper articles and pamphlets, according to Florida Memory, the Florida Department of State's archive program. He turned into an avid fan of the crop and planted 35 acres to sell as fodder. In the 1930s and 1940s, the Soil Conservation Service promoted kudzu as a means of stabilizing soil in the rapidly eroded gullies of the South, particularly in the Piedmont regions of Alabama, Georgia, and Mississippi. The agency distributed more than 85 million seedlings and paid farmers to plant the vine. The farmers were paid to plant kudzu, and more than 1.2 million acres were planted under this federal program. This number covers only the acreage planted under the federal program, not all the kudzu planted in the U.S., and Bill Finch's reporting in Smithsonian Magazine puts total plantings at a little more than a million acres by 1945.Kudzu's growth rate rises with carbon dioxide, and it spends little on woody tissueWhy did the vine take so well? Kudzu (Pueraria montana): History, Physiology, and Ecology Combine to Make a Major Ecosystem Threat, published in Critical Reviews in Plant Sciences in 2004, offers part of the answer. The growth of kudzu is stimulated significantly by increased levels of CO₂, according to Irwin Forseth and Anne Innis of the University of Maryland, College Park. Because kudzu does not invest in woody structure, this growth boost could make it even more competitive as atmospheric CO₂ concentrations rise. A fast-growing plant that invests little in woody tissue can outcompete slower-growing rivals.Nitrogen fixation more than doubles nitric oxide emissions from invaded soilsThe plant also alters the soil it grows in. Jonathan Hickman and colleagues showed this in "Kudzu (Pueraria montana) Invasion Doubles Emissions of Nitric Oxide and Increases Ozone Pollution," published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences in 2010. The authors point to the southeastern United States as an area of particular concern: because kudzu fixes nitrogen, it drives extra nitric oxide emissions from the soil, and nitric oxide feeds ozone formation. In 2007, the team studied soils at three sites in Madison County, Georgia. In invaded soils, net nitrogen mineralization rose by up to 1,000% and net nitrification by up to 500% compared with control soils, and nitric oxide emissions were more than 100% higher (2.81 versus 1.24 ng NO‑N cm⁻² h⁻¹). Only these figures are field measurements.The researchers then fed their data into the GEOS‑Chem atmospheric chemistry model and assumed an extreme scenario in which kudzu invaded all nonagricultural, nonurban soils across nine southeastern states. Under that scenario, soil nitric oxide emissions rose by 28%, and some areas saw up to seven additional days each summer when 8-hour ozone concentrations exceeded 70 ppb. These are projections, not measurements.Forest Service survey data puts kudzu on about 227,000 acres of Southern forestlandKudzu is often said to cover seven million to nine million acres of the United States, but Bill Finch, writing in Smithsonian Magazine's "The True Story of Kudzu, the Vine That Never Truly Ate the South," reports that scientists reassessing its spread found nothing close to that. Forest Service survey data from 2010 shows that 227,000 acres of southern forestland contain kudzu, about one-tenth of 1 percent of the region's 200 million acres of forestland. This estimate covers forestland only, so kudzu growing on other land is not counted.The Forest Service expects the infested forestland to grow by no more than 2,500 acres a year, while some sources repeat an unsupported figure of 150,000 acres a year. The research on kudzu's ecology helps explain why the plant competes so well. Forseth and Innis (2004) attribute kudzu's edge to two physiological traits: a fast response to high CO₂ concentrations and little investment in woody tissue. Much of what people say about kudzu's ecological effects comes from testimony rather than measurement, which is why the Forest Service survey and the studies above matter. It was planted deliberately, its growth habits give it a competitive edge, and its effects on soil chemistry reach as far as the air above it. Its environmental impact is smaller than some legends suggest.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
